plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure sets four triangle sketches in a row, labeled (a) through (d) below, to enumerate the possible outcomes when two sides and a non-included angle are known. All four share one labeling scheme: an acute angle alpha marked by an arc at the left end of a horizontal base, a vertex beta at the right end of that base, an apex gamma above, side b rising from alpha to gamma, and side a hanging from gamma. Panel (a), headed No triangle, a < h, draws a as a short vertical segment from gamma that stops above the base, leaving a visible gap so nothing closes. Panel (b), headed Right triangle, a = h, has a reaching the base exactly at beta, with a small square marking the right angle formed there. Panel (c), headed Two triangles, a > h, a < b, shows a solid vertical altitude labeled h from gamma to the base, plus two dashed segments each labeled a running from gamma to different landing points, one to the left of the altitude's foot and one at beta. Panel (d), headed One triangle, a is greater than or equal to b, shows a broad triangle whose side a slopes from gamma down to beta. Aligning the four under identical labels isolates the one quantity that changes, the length of a measured against the altitude and against b, and shows how many closures each case admits.

interactionPlan.concept: In the SSA (side–side–angle) configuration, the known angle α and side b fix vertex γ, so the unknown side a acts like a compass arc swung from γ — and whether it misses the base, touches it once, or crosses it twice decides whether zero, one, or two triangles exist.
elements: Horizontal base line (side c) drawn as a solid ray starting at the left vertex and extending to the right
Left vertex with a small arc marking the given acute angle, labeled α
Side b drawn as a solid straight segment rising from the left vertex to the apex, labeled b
Apex vertex labeled γ
Right vertex where side a meets the base, labeled β
Side a drawn from the apex down to the base, labeled a
Dashed altitude segment from the apex perpendicular to the base, labeled h, with a small right-angle square at its foot
Dashed circular arc of radius a centered at the apex, sweeping down toward the base
Small hollow dots marking where the arc of radius a meets the base (none, one, or two)
Second (alternate) side a drawn dashed to the other intersection point when two solutions exist, with its own β' vertex label
Faint shading of the closed triangle(s) currently formed
Short caption text under the figure naming the current case in words and the inequality relating a, h, and b

interactions.teaches: That sweeping the single unknown length a carries the same construction continuously from no solution, through exactly one right-triangle solution, into two solutions, and back to one — with the switches happening precisely at a = h and a = b.
interactions.label: Length of the swinging side a (α and b held fixed)

interactions.teaches: That the perpendicular height h from γ to the base is the shortest reach possible, which is why a < h can never close a triangle and a = h closes exactly one right triangle.
interactions.label: Show altitude h

demo_steps.title: What is given
demo_steps.narration: Angle α and side b are known, so the apex γ is already pinned down; only the length of side a is free. The dashed altitude h drops from γ perpendicular to the base and marks the shortest distance γ can reach.

demo_steps.title: a shorter than h — no triangle
demo_steps.narration: When a is shorter than the altitude, the arc swung from γ stops above the base and a visible gap remains. No triangle can close, so the given parts describe no triangle at all.

demo_steps.title: a equal to h — one right triangle
demo_steps.narration: Grow a until it just equals h and the arc grazes the base at a single point, meeting it perpendicularly. Exactly one triangle exists, and it is a right triangle.

demo_steps.title: h < a < b — the ambiguous case
demo_steps.narration: For lengths between h and b the arc cuts the base in two places, so two different triangles share the same α, a, and b. This is the ambiguous SSA case.

demo_steps.title: a at least b — one triangle
demo_steps.narration: Once a reaches or exceeds b the second intersection falls behind the vertex at α, off the usable ray, so only one triangle survives.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Side a is a compass arc swung from γ, so the entire ambiguous-case rule is just geometry: compare a with h = b·sin α and with b, and the number of intersections with the base tells you how many triangles are possible.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: One clean, centered textbook-style construction in black line art on white. A horizontal base line runs left to right; at the left vertex a small arc marks angle α and a solid segment b rises to the apex γ. From γ a dashed arc of radius a sweeps down toward the base, with the resulting side a (and, when two solutions exist, a second dashed side a) drawn to the hollow intersection dots on the base, labeled β and β'. A thin dashed perpendicular from γ to the base is labeled h with a small right-angle square at its foot. Use italic serif math labels (α, β, γ, a, b, c, h) matching textbook typography; keep given parts black, the swinging side a in a contrasting accent color, and the altitude in a lighter dashed stroke. A single line of caption text below the figure states the current case in words. No extra panels, legends, or data tables beyond this caption.

authoredContext:
Oblique triangles in the category SSA may have four different outcomes. The figure illustrates the solutions with the known sides a and b and known angle α.

Four attempted oblique triangles are in a row, all with standard labels. Side c is the horizontal base. In the first attempted triangle, side a is less than the altitude height. Since side a cannot reach side c, there is no triangle. In the second attempted triangle, side a is equal to the length of the altitude height, so side a forms a right angle with side c. In the third attempted triangle, side a is greater than the altitude height and less than side b, so side a can form either an acute or obtuse angle with side c. In the fourth attempted triangle, side a is greater than or equal to side b, so side a forms an acute angle with side c.

plan.concept: When two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) are known, the number of triangles that can close depends entirely on how the swinging side a compares with the altitude h = b·sin(α) and with the side b.
elements: Row of four reference panels labeled (a), (b), (c), (d) beneath each sketch
Panel (a) heading: 'No triangle, a < h'
Panel (b) heading: 'Right triangle, a = h'
Panel (c) heading: 'Two triangles, a > h, a < b'
Panel (d) heading: 'One triangle, a ≥ b'
Shared labeling in every panel: horizontal base from α on the left to β on the right
Acute angle arc at α in every panel
Vertex label α (lower left), β (lower right), γ (apex, above)
Side b drawn as the solid ray from α up to γ, labeled b
Side a drawn hanging from γ, labeled a (short vertical stub not reaching the base in (a); vertical to β in (b); two dashed segments in (c); sloping to β in (d))
Small square right-angle marker at β in panel (b)
Solid vertical altitude segment from γ to the base labeled h in panel (c)
Visible gap between the end of side a and the base in panel (a)

Large live construction panel: fixed base ray from α, fixed angle α arc, fixed side b to γ, dashed altitude h from γ with foot marker, and a circular arc of radius a centered at γ sweeping toward the base
Intersection markers where the arc of radius a meets the base line (0, 1, or 2 hollow dots)
Readout box showing current a, h = b·sin α, b, and the resulting count: 0, 1, or 2 triangles
Highlight ring / colored outline on whichever of the four reference panels matches the current value of a
Legend: solid black = given parts (α, b, base); red = swinging side a; blue dashed = altitude h

interactions.teaches: That sweeping the single unknown length a carries the construction continuously through zero, one, two, and back to one solution, with the transitions occurring exactly at a = h and a = b.
interactions.label: Length of side a (α = 35°, b = 5, h ≈ 2.87)

interactions.teaches: That the altitude h = b·sin α is the shortest possible reach from γ to the base, so any a shorter than h simply cannot touch the base and any a equal to h touches it exactly once, perpendicularly.
interactions.label: Show altitude h and right-angle marker

interactions.teaches: That each of the four textbook panels is one snapshot of the same construction, tied to a specific inequality comparing a with h and b.
interactions.label: Step through the four cases

demo_steps.title: The fixed given parts
demo_steps.narration: Angle α and side b are locked in place, so vertex γ never moves; only the length of side a is unknown. The dashed altitude h drops from γ perpendicular to the base and marks the shortest distance γ can ever reach.

demo_steps.title: Case (a): a is too short
demo_steps.narration: With a = 2.0 and h ≈ 2.87, the arc of radius a swung from γ never reaches the base — a visible gap remains, exactly as in panel (a). No triangle can close.

demo_steps.title: Case (b): a exactly equals h
demo_steps.narration: Grow a to 2.87 and the arc just grazes the base at a single point, landing perpendicularly at β. The right-angle square appears: exactly one triangle, and it is a right triangle.

demo_steps.title: Case (c): the ambiguous case
demo_steps.narration: For a between h and b, the arc crosses the base in two places, giving two different closing segments — the two dashed sides a of panel (c). Both are valid triangles with the same α, a, and b.

demo_steps.title: Case (d): a is long enough to overtake b
demo_steps.narration: Once a reaches or passes b, the second intersection falls on the wrong side of α — behind the vertex — so only one triangle survives. Turn the altitude off and the sketch is just the ordinary triangle of panel (d).

plan.keyInsight: Side a is a compass arc swung from γ: whether it misses the base, touches it once, cuts it twice, or cuts it only once on the usable side is decided solely by comparing a with h = b·sin α and with b — that is the entire ambiguous SSA case.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Top band: the four original black-line panels in a horizontal row, all sharing the same labeling (horizontal base, arc at α on the left, β on the right, γ above, side b from α to γ, side a hanging from γ), each with its italic-math heading above and (a)–(d) centered below; panel (a) shows a short vertical a with a clear gap above the base, panel (b) shows a meeting the base at β with a small right-angle square, panel (c) shows a solid labeled altitude h plus two dashed segments each labeled a, panel (d) shows a broad triangle with a sloping down to β. Bottom (larger) area: one live construction at roughly twice the size — black base ray and black side b with the angle arc at α, blue dashed altitude h from γ with a small foot tick and right-angle square when a = h, a red arc of radius a centered at γ sweeping down toward the base, hollow red dots at each base intersection, and the resulting triangle(s) filled with faint red. A small readout in the corner prints a, h, b and 'triangles: 0 / 1 / 2'. The currently matching reference panel gets a soft yellow highlight box. Serif italic math labels (α, β, γ, a, b, h) throughout, matching the textbook typography.
